Research engineering / Global Structure-from-Motion

GLIMMER.

Global Image Matching with Effective Measurement Reduction, bringing MAC-based spectral edge selection from pose-graph SLAM to GLOMAP's image view graphs.

C++GLOMAPStructure-from-MotionSpectral SparsificationView Graphs
01 / Problem

Which image matches should a reconstruction retain?

Global Structure-from-Motion estimates camera poses from a network of pairwise image relationships. As the number of images grows, the view graph can contain many relative measurements, increasing the work required by downstream estimation.

GLIMMER explores a graph-theoretic approach: preserve a connected backbone, then select a budgeted subset of additional image-pair measurements based on their contribution to spectral connectivity.

Can MAC-style edge selection reduce view-graph measurements while retaining useful global connectivity for reconstruction?
02 / Approach

From dense view graph to selected measurements

The repository describes a C++ port of MAC-based view-graph sparsification (Algorithm 3) into GLOMAP. GLOMAP (Pan, Barath, Pollefeys & Schönberger, 2024) estimates camera rotations, then camera and point positions, then refines everything with bundle adjustment; GLIMMER's module runs earlier than all of that, right after the view graph itself is built.

GLOMAP'S PUBLISHED PIPELINE, WITH THE MAC INSERTION POINT MARKED

GLIMMER's MAC-based edge selection runs on the view graph right after correspondence search finishes (after view graph calibration and relative pose decomposition) and before global estimation begins (rotation averaging, global positioning, bundle adjustment, and structure refinement). Every downstream stage works from the sparsified edge set instead of the full dense graph.

01

Construct

Represent image-pair relationships as edges in a global view graph.

02

Optimize

Use MAC-inspired spectral edge selection to allocate a measurement budget.

03

Integrate

Bring the selected measurements into the GLOMAP-based SfM workflow.

03 / Engineering

Research algorithm → C++ system

The engineering focus is transferring MAC-based graph selection into a different problem setting. Pose-graph SLAM connects robot poses; global SfM connects camera views through pairwise image measurements. Both can be modeled as graphs, but their measurement representations and reconstruction pipelines differ.

GLIMMER's repository identifies its contribution as a C++ port of MAC-based view-graph sparsification (Algorithm 3) into GLOMAP. The project is best presented as an algorithm-integration effort, not as a new SfM pipeline built from scratch.

Research provenance. GLOMAP is an existing global Structure-from-Motion framework. This project builds on it; its upstream reconstruction capabilities and published performance figures should not be attributed to GLIMMER.
Explore GitHub repository ↗

Geller Hall: MST Backbone Reconstructions

Geller Hall is one of the two benchmark datasets used to validate this port (South Building is the other, shown further down). GLIMMER reconstruction visualizations for the Geller Hall dataset using an MST backbone at three measurement-budget settings. The screenshots show reconstructed 3D points and camera poses; they are qualitative visualizations, not quantitative accuracy comparisons.

The 99-edge MST backbone is retained in every run. The 30% and 50% budgets apply to the 718 remaining candidate edges, so total edge retention differs from the nominal candidate budget. All three runs use 100 images and 817 valid edges. The 30% matrix issue is reported but its cause is not yet confirmed.

South Building · MST backbone

125 images · 832 valid edges · 124-edge MST backbone. Budget percentages refer to the 708 non-backbone candidate edges.

04 / Evidence

What is established, and what needs validation

The public repository description establishes the intended MAC-to-GLOMAP port. Its visible README currently contains predominantly upstream GLOMAP documentation, so it does not independently establish reconstruction accuracy, runtime improvements, dataset benchmarks, or ablation results for GLIMMER.

A rigorous next step is to compare the selected view graphs with the full graph across edge budgets, reconstruction completeness, camera-pose quality, and computational cost.

Overall, MAC's edge-selection performance across the tested budgets is strong: it consistently retains a sparse backbone while keeping algebraic connectivity high, on both the Geller Hall and South Building datasets. Two things are still open. Execution time does not scale monotonically with budget on Geller Hall (77 s at 100%, 88 s at 50%, 65 s at 30%); the 50% run taking longer than the full 100% run is a real timing discrepancy I am still investigating, not an expected result. Second, this port currently runs the single-pass selection described above; the fully iterative MAC refinement loop (the repeated Frank–Wolfe optimization used in the research version) has not yet been tested in this C++ port.

ETH3D SLAM benchmark results reproduced from Pan, Barath, Pollefeys & Schönberger, “Global Structure-from-Motion Revisited,” 2024. These are GLOMAP's own published numbers against OpenMVG, Theia and COLMAP, not anything I measured. I haven't run GLIMMER on these ETH3D scenes yet; so far it's only been tested on the Geller Hall and South Building datasets shown above. Testing the MAC port on this same benchmark, so sparsification can be compared scene-by-scene against these published baselines, is planned next.

The research direction: select fewer image measurements without discarding the connectivity needed for global reconstruction.
